E0221.summary: One of the preparations the vulgar Matter undergoes; Synesius makes calcination a name of the single operation, the same as extracting soul, spirit or body.
E0221.body: Quoted from Synesius, calcination is one of the names of the single operation: “to extract the soul, or the spirit, or the body, is nothing else than the aforesaid calcinations” [III.3 ¶60], and these names are used “in regard they signify the operation of Venus” [III.3 ¶60]. Atwood herself lists calcinations among the preparations the vulgar Matter passes through before it becomes the Mercury of the Philosophers: “Hence all those preparations, solutions, calcinations, etc.” [II.2 ¶16]. Elsewhere she places it as a step before a reunion into permanent form: “after calcinations there is a reunion” [III.2 ¶64]. The text does not define the operation further.

E0222.summary: A king, initiated and converted, cited as author of the Liber Secretorum and as one of the Mahomedan princes agreed concerning the Matter.
E0222.body: Atwood cites Calid as a king who was initiated and converted and who wrote treatises, among them the *Liber Secretorum, or Secret of Secrets* [I.1 ¶35]. Later she counts him among “the Mahomedan princes” who agree concerning the Matter, using him as supporting testimony [III.2 ¶60].

E0223.summary: Dionysius's name for the primordial cloud, obscure and humanly incomprehensible though visible; called Tenebrae activae by the author of the Lumen de Lumine.
E0223.body: A quoted term: Dionysius's name for the primordial cloud, of which it is said “it is obscure and humanly incomprehensible, though visible indeed” and “a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm” [III.2 ¶13]. It is identified with the Kabalists' term: “The author of the Lumen de Lumine calls it, from the Kabalists, Tenebrae activae” [III.2 ¶13], described as beneath all sense and imagination.

E0224.summary: Author whose Hymn to Minerva and Hymn to Apollo Atwood quotes on the purity Divinity requires.
E0224.body: Atwood quotes Callimachus's *Hymn to Minerva* in support of the point that Divinity rejects anything mixed: “All mixture of her pure and simple oil” [III.2 ¶64; III.2 ¶65; III.2 n48]. She quotes the *Hymn to Apollo* (in Dodd's version) to illustrate the coming of the God of Light and the purity required to behold him: “Apollo’s eyes endure None but the good, the perfect, and the pure.” [IV.2 ¶37; IV.2 ¶38; IV.2 n26]. In both cases she uses him approvingly as illustration.

E0225.summary: Where the conflux of the water below and the ether above takes place, and from which the physical Tetractys springs.
E0225.body: Atwood says the meeting of the water below and the ether above happens in a Calx: “the conflux of these two is in a Calx” [III.3 ¶72]; from it the physical Tetractys springs. The term is not further defined.

E0226.summary: In a saying of Hermes, that which rests on the fire, itself a fiery flame, and is corrupted in the heat of the boiling fire.
E0226.body: A quoted term from Hermes: that which rests on the fire, itself a fiery flame — “that which in the heat of the boiling fire is corrupted is Cambar” [I.3 ¶42]. Not further explained.

E0227.summary: Author of Antiquities, cited as describing the Nobles of the Rose coins.
E0227.body: Atwood cites Camden's *Antiquities* in support, as describing the Nobles of the Rose coins [I.1 ¶47].

E0229.summary: The ashes in which the principle of body is preserved and from which the whole life is restored; also an epithet of the Matter.
E0229.body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “what they call the ashes or Caput Mortuum” [APP ¶26] as where the principle of body is preserved; from that one principle the whole life is restored. She reports that Khunrath has other names for it: “Khunrath call it ‘our pigmy’, also the ‘diadem of the body’” [APP ¶26], and tentatively adds “I think he refers to it under the term Duanach” [APP ¶26].

In the main text, quoting Synesius and the New Light, caput mortuum is one of the epithets of the Matter: “O our caput mortuum, or dead head, or foeces of our sea!” [I.2 ¶33].

E0230.summary: Atwood's hedged name for Reason investigating her First Source.
E0230.body: Atwood names the process she has described, with the hedge 'it would seem', “the Catholic Art of Reason investigating her First Source” [IV.2 ¶21].

E0231.summary: What the Hermetic experiment arrives at, passing from either extreme of mind and matter, where external and internal worlds blend.
E0231.body: Atwood says the Hermetic experiment, “as passing from whither extreme of Mind and matter, to prove them, it arrives at the Catholic Effect of Life” [IV.4 ¶11]; there the external and internal worlds blend.

E0232.summary: For some modern Kabalists, the universal germ before birth, seen as a nebulous cloud; a concentration of Divinity that gives birth to the primitive Ether.
E0232.body: A view Atwood reports from some modern Kabalists: the universal germ before its birth appears as a cloud — “This nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo before its birth” [III.2 ¶13] — an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity, giving birth to the primitive Ether.

E0233.summary: 'That which is sown' in man: it contains all things and must die before it is quickened.
E0233.body: Atwood glosses 'that which is sown' in man: “that which is sown (viz., the catholic germ of his existence” [I.3 n8]. It contains all things and must die before it is quickened.

E0234.summary: The universal nature that is the subject of the Art: precious when exalted, defiled and despised in the common world.
E0234.body: Atwood: “The same catholic nature, which in its preternatural exaltation appears so very precious” [I.3 n40] is, in the common world, defiled and despised. The context presents it as the subject of the Art.

E0235.summary: Something miraculously kindled that kindles the Light of Universal Nature, acting through the three kingdoms and rejoicing most in the Mind of Man.
E0235.body: Atwood: “The catholic torch, miraculously kindled, kindles the Light of Universal Nature” [IV.4 ¶32]; it acts through the three kingdoms by voluntary assimilation and rejoices most in the Mind of Man. The text does not identify it further.

E0236.summary: In the Table Talk, where the individual light of life is lodged, driving adhering evil to the extremities and freeing the threefold life to ascend.
E0236.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of the time “when the individual light of life is lodged in its causal center” [APP ¶150]: adhering evil is then precipitated to the extremities and the threefold life is freed to ascend.

E0237.summary: Knowledge of cause, the only thing that fulfils the Idea of Truth, superior to the exhibition of phenomena.
E0237.body: Atwood holds that “neither can anything short of the Causal Discovery fulfill the Idea of Truth” [IV.4 ¶13]; it ranks above the mere exhibition of phenomena, the only doubt being whether it is possible. The adjacent passage speaks of knowledge “leading out from the Causal Fountain into natural effect” [IV.4 ¶12]. See also Causal Knowledge.

E0238.summary: The source of all things and of Wisdom, from which riches come and whose emanative splendour the true gods are.
E0238.body: Atwood speaks of “riches as from the Causal fountain of all things” [II.4 ¶19], and of the true gods “as an emanative splendour from the Causal Fountain, make manifest in energy its Intellectual Law” [II.4 ¶29]. It is also the source of Wisdom, to be approached by prayer as one applies to a master of an art: “the Causal Fountain for Wisdom, which is His alone and voluntarily to bestow” [III.4 ¶20].

E0239.summary: Knowledge of causes, the worthiest part of knowledge, without which external science leaves us no wiser; withheld from the unworthy.
E0239.body: Atwood insists the unworthy be kept from it, lest they handle 'the powerful machine of nature' for selfish ends: “these are unfit to be admitted to the Causal Knowledge” [I.3 n10]. Without it external science leaves us no wiser: “what would we be wiser without the Causal knowledge of these things?” [IV.4 ¶29]; and “For the discovery of the Causal Nature is doubtless of all parts of knowledge the worthiest to be sought after” [IV.4 ¶32]. See also Causal Discovery.

E0240.summary: The light within a person, which the Art draws forth, fixes and brings to manifestation; nature's Causal Light reached through the Understanding.
E0240.body: Atwood identifies it with what is within: “That which is within, viz., the causal light, must be drawn forth by art and fixed” [I.3 n8]. The Art aims to “bring the Causal light to manifestation” [II.1 ¶17], and to recover “the Ancient Experiment of nature into her Causal Light” [III.4 ¶2]. It is reached by rational permeation, “by the Understanding of Nature, into her Causal Light” [IV.1 ¶20]. The goal includes knowing the First Truth experimentally and being able “to revolve the Causal Light in permanence of intellection” [IV.4 ¶22]. Beyond the identification with 'that which is within', the text does not define it.

E0241.summary: In Hermes (Asclepius), something man can both find and effect.
E0241.body: Quoting Hermes in the Asclepius: “man should be able not only to find the Causal Nature but to effect it” [III.1 ¶21]. Atwood also calls its discovery the worthiest part of knowledge [IV.4 ¶32] (see Causal Knowledge).

E0242.summary: The goal of the ancients' method of ascent, surveyed more or less immediately after gradual assimilation.
E0242.body: Atwood describes the ancients' ascent as proceeding by gradual assimilation “to a survey more or less immediate of the Causal Source” [III.2 ¶33].

E0243.summary: The truth of causes, as opposed to remote effects, beheld in the apperceptive vision granted to those proved and reproved.
E0243.body: Atwood contrasts it with remote effects, speaking of those “who have never glanced even in imagination toward the Causal Truth” [II.1 ¶49]; it is drawn from a deep well. It is what is beheld when Light meets Light, by those proved and reproved “previous to being admitted to the apperceptive vision of the Causal Truth which they describe” [III.2 ¶28].

E0244.summary: Four causes — essence, matter, origin of motion, and end — which in the Art pass into one another; cause is not mere antecedence in time.
E0244.body: Atwood names four causes: essence (the principle, 'First Why'); matter or subject; that whence motion begins; and “That for the sake of which the inquiry subsists, and the Good which is the end of regeneration” [IV.2 ¶7]. In the Art the First becomes efficient in the Third and passes by the Second into the Fourth [IV.2 ¶7]. She rejects attempts to “reduce the Idea of Cause to mere antecedence or juxtaposition in time” [IV.4 ¶15], citing the testimony of instinct, and says this science “exhibits all things in their constructive Causes” [IV.4 ¶22].

E0245.summary: A place to be entered with prudent motive, from which the mineral radix of the Art is carried away; by Hermetic interpretation, Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life.
E0245.body: Atwood gives the Hermetic interpretation: “the Cave of Mercury, which, according to the Hermetic interpretation, is Taenerus, the most hidden vapor of life” [III.1 ¶19]. It is to be entered with a prudent motive, and the mineral radix of the Art is carried away from it [III.1 ¶19].

E0246.summary: The prior Elements of Life the ancients actually investigated, as opposed to the common elements or abstractions.
E0246.body: Atwood says the ancients investigated not the common elements or abstractions but “the prior Elements of Life; which some, openly distinguishing, call the Celestial Elements” [III.2 ¶36].

E0247.summary: In the Table Talk, the emotional, receptive, instinctive life, representing the Vegetable Kingdom and seated in the epigastric region.
E0247.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The Celestial is the emotional, receptive, instinctive life, and represents the Vegetable Kingdom.” [APP ¶32]. It resides in the epigastric region, its workshop the solar plexus; it is identified with the medial life, through which the third life must be born [APP ¶32]. Compare celestial medial life.

E0248.summary: In Boehme, the light in which the Tincture is, containing a substance like water which is no water.
E0248.body: Quoting Boehme, the Tincture is in the Celestial Light: “And there is in the Celestial Light, continues the same author, a Substance like water which yet is no water” [III.2 ¶16].

E0249.summary: The intermediate life preceding the heroic work, which must be cut off, shut up and buried; until it dissolves the Vital Spirit cannot be radically improved.
E0249.body: Atwood speaks of “the celestial medial life which, in the order of divine rites, precedes the heroic work” [III.1 ¶26]. It must be cut off in its prime, shut up and buried; until “this dissolution of the first medial life” [III.1 ¶28] takes place, the Vital Spirit cannot be radically improved. Compare Celestial life, which the Table Talk identifies with the medial life [APP ¶32].

E0250.summary: Image of the incessant, repeated purifying labour that clears the wasted field of human life.
E0250.body: Atwood's image for the repeated purifying labour of the work, which serves “to clear the wasted field of human life, and harrow it for a more congenial growth” [IV.1 ¶9].

E0251.summary: In Rabbi Ben Jochai, the form in man on which the world subsists and by which man is the image of God, distinguished from apparent man.
E0251.body: Atwood says the Zohar “beams with the revelation of the celestial prototype in humanity” [II.1 ¶40]. Quoting Rabbi Ben Jochai, it is the form in man on which the world subsists and by which man is the image of God, distinct from apparent man: “on that form in man, which is the Celestial Prototype” [II.1 ¶42]; “no form, no world, could exist before the human prototype” [II.1 ¶42].
